\chapter{También --- Your First Word, Hidden Inside}
\label{ch:tambien}
\hlchaptermodality{219}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can agree with what somebody just said, in two words.}

I can agree with what somebody just said, in two words.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[también]{también — a word with your very first word inside it}

\label{lesson:ES-C58-tambien}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Pero} sets two things against each other. Now the opposite move: adding one thing \textbf{to} another.

And say \emph{bien}, from your first chapter. You will need it in a moment, in a place you would not expect.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{accent-mark} — the accent on \textbf{también} puts the stress on the last syllable: \emph{tam-BYEN}.
  \item \texttt{b-soft} — the \emph{b} here is gentle, the lips barely closing.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{también} = \textbf{tan} + \textbf{bien}.

\emph{\textbf{Tan}} means \emph{so}, \emph{as} — it is the word Spanish uses to say how much of something there is. And \emph{\textbf{bien}} you have had since chapter one.

So \emph{también} is, literally, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}so well\textquotedblright{}}. Somebody says a thing; you say \emph{and that goes so well for me too}. Say it enough times and it stops being a comment about how well anything is going, and becomes the plain word for \emph{also}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Estudio español. Trabajo \textbf{también}.}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The most useful shape it takes is the shortest one:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{Estoy cansado.} — \emph{\textbf{Yo también.}}
\end{quote}

Two words, and you have agreed with somebody. That is worth more in a real conversation than most of the grammar in this book, and it costs nothing to remember, because you already knew half of it.

Notice the accent, too. It is there because \emph{también} is stressed on its last syllable, which is where the \emph{bien} sits — the borrowed half kept the stress it had when it was a word of its own.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Yo también}
  \item \emph{Estudio español. Trabajo también.}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{también}, taken apart? (\emph{\textbf{Tan}} \textbf{+} \emph{\textbf{bien}} — \emph{so well}.)

And which half have you known since the very beginning? (\emph{\textbf{Bien}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
